```{r libs}
library(agetime)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
```

This vignette describes problems that users commonly run into
when working with age, period, and cohort labels, and explains
how to solve them.


# Reading labels

## "Don't know how to interpret label"

### Problem

A label is not in any format that `agetime` recognizes.

```{r unparsed-problem, error = TRUE}
x <- c("0-4", "5-9", "Age not stated4", "85+ (a)")
age_standard(x)
```

### Solution

First, find the labels that cannot be parsed. Setting `interpret_fail`
to `"silent"` turns unparsable labels into `NA`, so they can be
compared with labels that really are missing.

```{r unparsed-find}
lower <- age_lower(x, interpret_fail = "silent")
is_missing <- age_is_missing(x, interpret_fail = "silent")
x[is.na(lower) & !is_missing]
```

Then clean the labels before passing them to `agetime`. Labels in published
tables often carry footnote markers, such as the `4` in `"Age not stated4"`
and the `(a)` in `"85+ (a)"`.

```{r unparsed-clean}
x_clean <- x |>
  sub(pattern = " \\(.*\\)$", replacement = "") |>
  sub(pattern = "([a-z])[0-9]+$", replacement = "\\1")
age_standard(x_clean)
```

### Discussion

`agetime` recognizes many common formats, including:

- ranges such as `"5-9"`, `"5 to 9"`, `"5--9"`, and `"5-9 years"`;
- open age groups such as `"85+"`, `"85 and over"`, `"85 or more"`,
  `"85 years and older"`, and `"85 & over"`;
- age groups starting at 0, such as `"Under 5"`, `"less than 5"`, `"<5"`,
  and `"Infant"`;
- totals such as `"Total"` and `"All ages"`, and missing values such
  as `"Not stated"`, `"Unknown"`, and `"Age not stated"`.

Case, spaces, and leading zeros do not matter. Labels containing decimals,
such as `"2.5"`, are not recognized.


## Numbers that are lower limits of wider age groups

### Problem

Ages are stored as numbers, such as `0`, `5`, `10`, ..., `85`, where
each number is the lower limit of a five-year age group, and `85` is the
lower limit of an open age group. `agetime` reads each number as a
single year of age.

```{r numbers-problem}
age <- c(0, 5, 10, 80, 85)
age_upper(age)
```

### Solution

Treat the numbers as single years, coarsen them to five-year groups, and
then make the last group open.

```{r numbers-solution}
age |>
  age_coarsen_five() |>
  age_set_open_right(at = 85)
```

For life-table age groups, where the numbers are `0`, `1`, `5`, `10`, ...,
use `age_coarsen_life()` in place of `age_coarsen_five()`.


## One-year periods written as ranges

### Problem

A period label such as `"2020-2021"` gives an error.

```{r one-year-problem, error = TRUE}
period_standard("2020-2021")
```

### Solution

By default, period and cohort functions read `"2020-2021"` as the
interval from the start of 2020 to the start of 2021, which is a single
year. `agetime` asks for single years to be written as `"2020"`.
If the data provider meant two years, 2020 and 2021, set `interpret_multi`
to `"below_upper"`.

```{r one-year-solution}
period_standard("2020-2021", interpret_multi = "below_upper")
```

### See Also

- The section on rules for interpreting inputs in `?period_lower`


## Financial and academic years: "Lower limit greater than upper limit"

### Problem

Labels such as `"2019/20"` or `"2019-20"`, used for financial or
academic years that start part-way through a calendar year,
give an error. `agetime` reads them as ranges that end before
they start.

```{r fiscal-problem, error = TRUE}
period_standard(c("2019/20", "2020/21"))
```

### Solution

`agetime` does not read these labels directly. Instead, label each
year by the calendar year in which it ends, and set `interpret_single`
to `"upper"`. With `"upper"`, the label `"2020"` describes the year
ending at 2020.

```{r fiscal-solution}
fy <- c("2019/20", "2020-21", "1999/00")
fy_end <- as.character(as.integer(substr(fy, 1L, 4L)) + 1L)
fy_end
period_lower(fy_end, interpret_single = "upper")
period_upper(fy_end, interpret_single = "upper")
```

The same approach works for cohorts, such as people born in a
particular financial year.

### Discussion

`agetime` represents periods using whole years, so a financial year
running from July to June is approximated by the year in which it ends.

### See Also

- The section on rules for interpreting inputs in `?period_lower`
  and `?cohort_lower`


## Non-calendar years next to open intervals: "2020" and "2020+"

### Problem

With non-calendar years, such as financial years running from July to
June, labels such as `"2020"` and `"2020+"` can look as if they overlap,
or a set of labels can appear to have a gap.

### Solution

Use `period_interval()` to see how `agetime` reads the labels.

```{r noncalendar-intervals}
period_interval(c("2019", "2020", "2020+"), interpret_single = "upper")
```

With `interpret_single = "upper"`, `"2020"` is the year ending at 2020,
that is, `[2019, 2020)`, which might be July 2019 to June 2020. An open
label such as `"2020+"` starts at 2020, which might be July 2020. So
`"2020"` and `"2020+"` do not overlap.

Some data providers use `"2020+"` to mean the year ending in 2020 and
all later years. Labels such as `"2018"`, `"2019"`, and `"2020+"` then
appear to have a gap, since nothing covers the year ending in 2020.

```{r noncalendar-gap}
labels <- c("2018", "2019", "2020+")
period_diagnose(labels, no_gap = TRUE, interpret_single = "upper")
```

To fix this, change `"2020+"` to `"2019+"`, which starts where the year
ending in 2020 starts.

```{r noncalendar-fix}
labels[labels == "2020+"] <- "2019+"
period_interval(labels, interpret_single = "upper")
```

### Discussion

`agetime` reads open labels such as `"2020+"`, `"2020 or more"`, and
`"<2020"` in the same way whatever the value of `interpret_single`, so
that they always describe the same interval.

### See Also

- [Financial and academic years](#financial-and-academic-years-lower-limit-greater-than-upper-limit)
- `period_interval()` and `cohort_interval()`
- The section on rules for interpreting inputs in `?period_lower`
  and `?cohort_lower`


## "Under", "less than", and "or earlier"

### Problem

Labels such as `"Under 5"`, `"<2000"`, and `"2000 or earlier"` mean
different things in different contexts.

### Solution

`agetime` uses the following rules:

- For ages, `"Under 5"`, `"less than 5"`, and `"<5"` all describe the
  age group from 0 to 4. Ages cannot be negative, so these age groups
  are closed.
- For periods and cohorts, `"before 2000"`, `"under 2000"`, and `"<2000"`
  describe everything before the start of 2000. `"2000 or earlier"` and
  `"up to 2000"` include 2000.
- For periods and cohorts, `"2000+"`, `"2000 or more"`, and
  `"2000 or later"` describe everything from the start of 2000 on.

```{r under}
age_standard(c("Under 5", "<5"))
cohort_standard(c("Under 2000", "2000 or earlier"))
period_standard(c("2000 or more", "2000 or later", "2000+"))
```

### Discussion

`"or older"` and `"or younger"` are recognized for ages, but not for periods
or cohorts, where they are ambiguous: an older cohort is an earlier one.

`"after 2000"` is not recognized. Read literally, it describes
everything from the start of 2001 on, but it is often used to mean
2000 and later years.

### See Also

- The section on rules for interpreting inputs in `?period_lower`
  and `?cohort_lower`


# Checking labels

## Different labels for the same age group

### Problem

`age_assert()` or `age_diagnose()` reports an overlap, even though
the age groups look distinct.

```{r synonyms-problem, error = TRUE}
x <- c("0", "infant", "1-4", "5+")
age_assert(x, no_overlap = TRUE)
```

### Solution

Two different labels, `"0"` and `"infant"`, describe the same age group.
Standardize the labels first.

```{r synonyms-solution}
x |>
  age_standard() |>
  age_assert(no_overlap = TRUE)
```

### Discussion

Repeated copies of the same label, as in a data frame with one row per
age group and sex, do not count as overlapping.


## Totals and missing values

### Problem

A check fails, or a coarsening function gives an error, because the
labels include a total or a missing value.

```{r totals-problem, error = TRUE}
x <- c("0-4", "5-9", "Total")
age_assert(x, no_total = TRUE)
```

### Solution

Remove totals and missing values before checking or coarsening, using
`age_is_total()` and `age_is_missing()`.

```{r totals-solution}
df <- tibble(
  age = c("0-4", "5-9", "Total", "Not stated"),
  count = c(10, 20, 35, 5)
)

df |>
  filter(!age_is_total(age), !age_is_missing(age))
```

### See Also

- Cookbook: [Drop totals from a dataset](cookbook.html#drop-totals) and
  [Drop "Not stated" categories from a dataset](cookbook.html#drop-missing)


## Checks that pass when they should fail

### Problem

`age_assert()` passes on a subset of a factor, such as a group in a grouped
data frame, even though the subset does not meet the condition.

### Solution

For factors, the `diagnose` and `assert` functions check levels, including
unused levels. Use `age_diagnose_values()` or `age_assert_values()` to
check only the values that are present.

### See Also

- Cookbook: [Check the values in a factor, ignoring unused levels](cookbook.html#validate-labels-values)


# Transforming labels

## Coarsening fails

### Problem

`age_coarsen()`, `age_coarsen_to()`, or one of their variants gives an
error.

```{r coarsen-problem, error = TRUE}
x <- c("0-4", "5-9", "12")
age_coarsen(x, breaks = c(0, 7, 10))
```

### Solution

The error message distinguishes two problems:

- A label *would be split* when it overlaps two or more new age groups,
  as `"5-9"` overlaps `"0-6"` and `"7-9"`. Move the breaks so that they
  fall between the old age groups.
- A label is *not fully covered* when it lies partly or wholly outside the
  new age groups, as `"12"` lies above 10. Add breaks, or, for
  `age_coarsen()`, set `open_right = TRUE`.

```{r coarsen-solution}
age_coarsen(x, breaks = c(0, 10), open_right = TRUE)
```

With `age_coarsen_to()`, every label must lie inside one of the labels in
`to`. Add labels to `to`, or remove labels that should not be included.


## Unused levels disappear from tables

### Problem

After adding levels with a `fill` function, `count()` or `summarise()`
still leaves out age groups with no observations.

### Solution

Tidyverse functions drop unused factor levels by default. Use
`.drop = FALSE`.

### See Also

- Cookbook: [Include levels that don't appear in the data](cookbook.html#fill-levels)


## Results are factors, not character vectors

### Problem

`age_coarsen()`, `age_fill()`, `age_set_open_right()`, and `age_set_order()`
return factors, which can be unexpected.

### Solution

These functions return factors so that levels, including unused ones, are
kept in the right order. Use `as.character()` if a character vector is
needed. `age_standard()` returns a character vector when its input is a
character vector, and a factor when its input is a factor.


## Midpoints of open age groups

### Problem

`age_mid()` gives an error for an open age group within a grouped
calculation.

```{r mid-problem, error = TRUE}
df <- tibble(
  sex = c("F", "F", "M"),
  age = c("80-84", "85+", "85+")
)

df |>
  mutate(mid = age_mid(age), .by = sex)
```

### Solution

`age_mid()` gives an open age group a midpoint based on the width of the
nearest closed age group. In the group `sex = "M"`, there is no closed age
group. Calculate midpoints before grouping.

```{r mid-solution}
df |>
  mutate(mid = age_mid(age))
```
